title: The Cold Case
blurb: 1969 to the late 1970s. One straight cut can never solve exclusive-or; two cuts can, but nobody in the mainstream knows how to train them (in Japan, Amari has a method, little known in the West), and a famous book calls the extension sterile. A cold year, two lamps on sills, a handwritten dedication, a British report, and the fair question of how much one book is to blame. A few windows stay lit in the snow, one of them over a thesis about rounding errors; and at the rim of the light a tall young man sits down.

shots.setting: parchment plate: four lanterns at the corners of a square, and a pair of scissors (timeless; 1969 in the story)

lines.text: The book’s simplest puzzle: exclusive-or. Light up if one input is on, not both. On a square, the lit cases sit at opposite corners.
lines.direction: slow, laying out a puzzle on the table, picking up the thread from 'a book about what one layer could never do'; a small comma-pause before 'not both'; 'On a square' slower, as if drawing it

lines.text: No straight cut can separate them.
lines.direction: matter-of-fact; then let the scissors try in silence

lines.text: Two cuts can: a hidden layer, cells between input and answer. Nobody in the mainstream knew how to train one.
lines.direction: three short steps; 'cells between input and answer' plain and explanatory, a gloss in passing; a small drop on the last sentence

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: four lanterns on a square, two lit at opposite corners: one scissor cut can never separate them, two hidden cuts can. crossfadeMood candleAmber→labGreen, 0.6–0.8 s, no dip, under the paper wipe from the board. CHAPTER INDEX TAB (the film's chapter-card device for clue chapters): at the shot's first frame a manila index tab, typed in Special Elite with the chapter title 'The Cold Case', drops down from the frame's top edge at TOP-left like a file-divider tab, holds for 2.5 seconds over the picture, and slides back up (top-left, so it never shares the bottom-left corner with the date stamp); no new shot, no lamp change. The paper-fold wipe carries the board's book-shadow to a parchment plate, ink on paper, camera locked. The teaching machine xorPlate: four ink paper lanterns at the corners of a square plot, the pair at (0,1) and (1,0) lit (warm halos), the pair at (0,0) and (1,1) dark. A small label 'exclusive or' and the truth table in a corner chip. On L0402 a pair of black paper scissors makes ONE straight cut that sweeps through many angles and positions (xorPlate sweep 0→1); a ring marks every lantern on the wrong side, and a counter in the margin ('on the wrong side:') never drops below 1, ticking 1, 2, 1, 2, 1. The sweep runs through the silent pause. On 'Two cuts' the scissors make two cuts (the two hidden units' real cut lines from the trained XOR net, solve 0→1); the diagonal band between them washes in lamplight and holds exactly the two lit lanterns. On 'hidden layer' the paper folds (fold 0→1): the lanterns move into the hidden units' space, where one straight cut now separates them; on 'between input and answer' the fold's middle crease glows faintly as the in-between row of cells (no caption; the narration names it). On 'Nobody in the mainstream knew how to train one' the scissors lift off the plate and hang, unmoving, over it: the cuts are drawn, not learned; the closing label (in Japan, Amari had a method; 'mainstream' is spoken, so the label needs no more) sets in on 'mainstream', before the scissors lift. The margin counter is part of the diagram (its caption 'on the wrong side:' only); no other captions besides the two listed labels. TEXT RULE: besides the chapter index tab (top-left) and the date stamp (bottom-left), at most two text items; the closing label appears on 'mainstream' and holds through the silent hold.

shots.setting: MIT, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1969: a quote card; then the paper stage, the 1969 candle lit beside a giant book

lines.text: In 1969, Minsky and Papert’s book proved what one layer cannot do.
lines.direction: even, respectful; this is real mathematics
lines.spoken: In nineteen sixty-nine, Minsky and Papert’s book proved what one layer cannot do.

lines.text: For many layers, it offered only what it called “our intuitive judgment that the extension is sterile”, while naming it a problem worth settling. A third candle: many layers are a dead end.
lines.direction: 'what it called' marks the book's own words for the ear; read the quote exactly and without irony; a beat before 'sterile'; 'while naming it a problem worth settling' fair and plain (the book asked for the question to be settled); then a breath, and the candle line plain and quiet, like the earlier candle lightings

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: Minsky and Papert's giant book and its 'sterile' quote card; the third candle, MANY-LAYERED NETS ARE A STERILE EXTENSION, is lit. CAMERA: stage only (the third candle is lit on the stage in front of the book; no study visit). Tint crossfade to duskRose. A huge book stands upright on the paper stage like a monolith, its cover blank but for one word cut in light, PERCEPTRONS. Two figures in profile beside it, Minsky (1960s puppet, older than in ch03) and Papert, standing, neither lit as villains: both in the same warm light. Name cards for both. On L0405 the quote card rises from the book's open last chapter, set in Special Elite, cut to the fragment the narrator reads. On 'third' (the narrator lights it aloud, as with every belief candle) a new candle is lit in front of the book, lettered MANY-LAYERED NETS ARE A STERILE EXTENSION, a clean new candle with no fray; a tiny tag at its base reads '1969'. CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). The sleeves are the bars of the chart: a longer sleeve means a belief held longer. A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim. Here the candle is new: no sleeve yet, only the full stub with its flame at the top ring. In the hold (wordless, no new text), the camera stays on the new flame and the two authors in the same warm light; the candle burns steadily. The oxblood question card is NOT swapped here; it changes at the end of the chapter (ch04-s08).

shots.setting: Britain, 1972–73: a raised lecture platform, then a televised debate in a steeply raked lecture theatre (the Royal Institution, London)

lines.text: In 1973, James Lighthill’s report for Britain blamed “the combinatorial explosion”. It struck rules far more than nets. Yet British funding fell for almost a decade.
lines.direction: crisp, neutral; Lighthill is a serious man, not a foil; three short sentences; 'It struck rules' lands clearly, a wink at the board's first suspect, not a gibe; a small lift on 'far more than nets'; 'Yet' plain

lines.text: One book's fault? Historians still argue; there were several blows.
lines.direction: fair-minded; the question genuinely open; even on 'several blows'

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: Lighthill at his lectern and the televised debate below; his report's middle box is struck, cards flutter onto the desk, and snow thickens at the windows. A steeply raked horseshoe theatre of wooden benches in silhouette, a single lectern on a raised platform lit from above. Lighthill (standing, profile, at the lectern) with a sheaf of papers; below him, seated in the pit, Donald Michie and two other opponents leaning forward. A television camera on a tripod in the right foreground (generic 1970s studio camera, no logo), its tally lamp a low-chroma ember (emberRed mixed about 60% into winterBlue), the only warm light. Name cards for Lighthill and Michie; a place stamp. The narrator speaks Lighthill's quoted phrase, so no quote card for it here. On 'explosion' the phrase is glossed wordlessly: on the sheaf in Lighthill's hand a tiny ink branching tree grows from one dot, each branch splitting in two, then in two again, faster each time, until the page is black with branches (choices multiplying faster than any search); no caption, and it is gone by the time the four cards fall. On 'rules' the camera glances down to his top page: three inked boxes, A, B, C, with only B (Building Robots, the general-purpose bridge) struck through and C (neural models among them) untouched; letters only, no caption. On 'fell' the backlight drops a step and snow thickens outside the high windows. On L0410's last word, 'decade', a quote card rises above the lectern and stays through the question and the whole wordless hold: Papert's 'Snow White' sentence in full, verbatim (“We did not think of our work as killing Snow White; we saw it as a way to understand her.” — Papert, 1988). It is the defendant's own testimony on the charge that one book killed the field ('Snow White' was his figure for neural-net research), so it rises as the narrator asks 'One book's fault?', and is read under near-silent music. On L0411 the camera stays in the theatre (in-world, winterBlue, no board and no mood change) and eases in on the lectern; on 'Historians' four small cards of equal size flutter down from the dark above and land on the lectern's sloped desk beside Lighthill's papers, one after another in a row, the last landing on 'blows', each a separate blow: TRANSLATION 1966; MANSFIELD 1969; PERCEPTRONS 1969; LIGHTHILL 1973 (the book's card the same size as the others). TEXT RULE: besides the place stamp and the two name cards, only the four-card row and Papert's quote (the explosion gloss is a picture, not a caption).

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a snowbound winter map with a few lit windows; the camera finds Helsinki and pushes in on a student's printout about rounding errors. The Winter Map, a key image: a vast snowbound paper landscape at night under a pale moon, ridgelines layered in haze (L1–L4), snow still falling lightly, laid out with west at frame left and east at frame right. Far apart across it, small houses with single lit windows. The camera opens wide and drifts slowly from EAST to WEST (right to left), never whipping: all three windows stay in frame together until the push-in, and their tags fade in east to west from the first frame, so each is readable while the narrator speaks: first a window in Tokyo, FUKUSHIMA · TOKYO · 1979 (layered 'eyes', an ancestor of later vision nets); then, a little farther west in Japan, AMARI · 1967 (a way to train more than one layer, little known in the West; the camera lingers here a beat, the same Amari named in the chapter's opening plate); then, farthest west across the dark, the window the camera settles on: HELSINKI · 1970. On 'clue', a faint thread of light rises from that window and hangs in the sky, unconnected to anything yet. On 'sat' the camera pushes in through the Helsinki window to a readable insert (held through 'rounding errors' until the pull-back): a student's silhouette (generic, unnamed) at a desk beside a stack of computer printout, the top sheet large in frame and legible as a few lines of FORTRAN-style code with ROUNDING ERRORS typed in its header (type well above the 26 px minimum). Just after the line (beat 'warm') the camera pulls back out of the window and up, past the map, to reveal in the foreground large warm houses with bright windows facing away from the map, their shadows thrown toward the viewer; nobody in them turns. TEXT RULE: besides the two short place tags (Tokyo, Helsinki), only the Amari tag and the Helsinki insert caption.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: Sussex, 1976: a tall young man sits at a desk at the very rim of the low winter candle's light, facing out; the question card is swapped and the chess slip curls overdue. CAMERA: stage (the desk at the rim), then BOARD (the C2-a pin and the Q1 swap as inserts), a WALL truck to W2, then back to the stage. Back on the candle stage, deep in winter: the sterile candle burns at centre, its pool of light small; snow drifts through the rim. CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). The sleeves are the bars of the chart: a longer sleeve means a belief held longer. A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim. Here: seven years held so far (1969 to 1976), so a seven-ring ghost sleeve (42 px) stands above the stub, faintly scored; its flame still live where sleeve meets stub, its rim clean. At the very rim of the light, right third, half in shadow, a plain wooden desk with a reading lamp switched off. A tall young man in 1970s dress (hinton-young: tall, slight, long-limbed) walks in from the dark on twos and SITS at the desk, facing out from the flame, his long shadow thrown across the floor. He is seated for the rest of the shot (never standing at the rim in this era). He is not named; no name card. On 'thirty-six' the camera eases slowly from the desk to the case board, and as it reaches the board the lamp tint-crossfades (crossfadeMood, 1.2 s, no dip) from winterBlue to candleAmber (STUDY LOCK: board and Wall are always candleAmber; the winter stays only in the snow seen past the study window): the hands pin the chapter's clue card (a pair of scissors making two cuts) into slot C2-a at the head of column C2 (per the staging appendix), and run a thread of light from it to the Helsinki card pinned just below it in the same column (the thread from s07 finally lands). Then, on 'light', on the oxblood thread along the top of the board, the hands unpin AND IF NO STRAIGHT LINE EXISTS? and pin in its place THEN HOW DO YOU TRAIN THE HIDDEN LAYER?: the chapter's open question, carried into ch05. Just after the line (beat 'chess'), a slow pan to the Wall of Forecasts, in its fixed slot order, quoted from BOARD MAP: its slots W1 to W8 left to right (W1 Turing, W2 chess, W3 Rosenblatt 1961, W4 Florence 2012, W5 Coulom, W6 the 30-to-50-years slip in shadow, W7 Hinton 2017, W8 an empty pin until ch15); in 1976 only W1 and W2 are pinned, the rest are empty pin-holes, and W6's slip hangs in shadow: the chess slip in the second slot, due 1968, has yellowed and its corner curls, its due-date tag now overdue; farther along, at W6, beyond the lamp's reach, one slip's corner shows half-lit, unreadable. Hold on the curled slip in candleAmber; then, as the camera returns to the desk at the rim, crossfadeMood back to winterBlue (1.2 s, no dip) and hold on the desk in the snow. TEXT RULE: besides the date stamp, only the chess slip's tag and the question card.
